clue.text: Irish broadcaster covering international ceremony

indicators.note: the broadcaster's letters are wrapped around the next piece, so covering signals one piece going inside another

parts.note: RTE is Raidió Teilifís Éireann, Ireland's national broadcaster

explanation.surface: An Irish TV channel broadcasting some international ceremony.
explanation.definitionFit: A rite is a formal religious or solemn act, a synonym for a ceremony.

clue.text: Check in ledger

definitions.meaning: to sign in on arrival, as at a hotel desk
a book of official records or accounts

explanation.surface: Checking something in a ledger.
explanation.definitionFit: To register is to check in on arrival, and a register is a ledger of records.

clue.text: Brilliant story, with editor accepting books

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so the books go inside

parts.note: a tale is a story
NT is the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A brilliant tale, with an editor taking on books for publication.
explanation.definitionFit: Talented means gifted, a synonym for brilliant in the sense of very able.

clue.text: Player's call after good drive comes to nothing

definitions.note: read as 'Player is', the 's joining definition to wordplay

indicators.note: the call piece is placed after the other pieces, so after orders the charade

parts.note: to drive something in is to ram it
O, the zero, stands for nothing
to call someone is to phone them

explanation.surface: A sports player's phone call after a good drive in golf or tennis comes to nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' suggests a sportsman; it is a record player. 'comes to' only links the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A gramophone is an old machine for playing records, a record player.

clue.text: Flower power's last hour on popular drug

indicators.note: last picks only the final letter of the word before it

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Flower power from the sixties, a late hour on a popular drug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is read as something that flows: a river.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhine is a great European river, and a river is a flower in the sense of a thing that flows.

clue.text: Lying urban reformer's promise may be this

parts.words: urban reformer's promise may be this
parts.note: split the answer into three words and it is what a town planner vows to do to a broken town

explanation.surface: A cynical view that an urban reformer's promises are just lies.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as MEND A CITY, it is the reformer's pledge; read whole, it is lying.
explanation.definitionFit: Mendacity is untruthfulness, the habit of telling lies.

clue.text: 22 Across moving right on past?

indicators.note: moving letters around rearranges them, so the three words are jumbled

explanation.surface: A defiant remark made while moving right on past someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points to the answer of 22 Across, a defiant last word.
explanation.definitionFit: A final cutting remark made on leaving is a parting shot, and that retort is one.

clue.text: Judgement needing time to replace popular alternative

indicators.note: the time letter takes the place of the popular word in the judgement

parts.note: an opinion is a judgement
in means popular or fashionable

explanation.surface: A judgement that needs time to replace a popular choice.
explanation.definitionFit: An option is a choice, one of several alternatives available.

clue.text: Dodgy cash job requiring student to start late

indicators.note: late means dead or gone, so the start of the student's word is gone

parts.note: a learner is a student, as in a learner driver

explanation.surface: A shady cash-in-hand job needing a student to start work late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'late' means 'former', so the opening L goes. A 'nice little earner' is British slang for a dodgy money-maker.
explanation.definitionFit: Earner is British slang for a profitable, often slightly shady, sideline paid in cash.

clue.text: Swallow in trepidation as promotion rejected

indicators.note: rejected is taken as sent back, so the word for promotion is read backwards

parts.note: a plug is a piece of publicity promoting something

explanation.surface: Someone gulps nervously as a hoped-for promotion is turned down.
explanation.definitionFit: To gulp is to swallow hard, often from nerves or fear.

clue.text: Graphic artist using a mixture of wire and string

indicators.note: a mixture blends things together, so the letters of the two words are mixed up

explanation.surface: An artist working with a jumble of wire and string, perhaps for a sculpture.
explanation.definitionFit: A signwriter paints lettering on signs and shopfronts, a kind of graphic artist.

clue.text: Time students must be backed with increase?

indicators.note: backed is taken as turned to face the other way, so the students' letters are read backwards

parts.note: NUS is the National Union of Students in the UK
a rise is an increase, as in a pay rise

explanation.surface: A question of when students should be supported with a grant increase.
explanation.walkthrough: NUS is the National Union of Students, the British student body.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunrise names a time of day, the moment the sun comes up.

clue.text: Doctor was not nice — a scientist

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are altered

explanation.surface: A doctor who was not nice, like a cold scientist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like the subject; it is the verb meaning tamper with.
explanation.definitionFit: He was the English physicist who formulated the laws of motion and gravity.

clue.text: Notice one model is fat

parts.note: an ad is a notice, as in a newspaper advertisement
I is the Roman numeral one
to model for an artist is to pose

explanation.surface: A notice saying one particular model is overweight.
explanation.definitionFit: Adipose describes body fat or fatty tissue, so it is a technical word for fat.

clue.text: Striking, oddly very English, and infectious

indicators.note: oddly signals taking alternate letters of the word very, leaving every other one

parts.note: an infectious disease is catching

explanation.surface: Something very English and infectious makes a striking impression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' picks the alternate letters E and Y from 'very' (its second and fourth).
explanation.definitionFit: Something eye-catching grabs attention, just as a striking design does.

clue.text: Case of late support for long-standing account

indicators.note: in a down clue, a supporting piece sits beneath the other

parts.note: chronic means long-lasting, as of an illness

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outer shell, its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A long-standing account of a late person's case history.
explanation.definitionFit: A chronicle is a historical record of events, so an account.

clue.text: Represented cadet, apparently?

parts.note: read the answer's first word with the second as an anagram signal: its letters let out give the word cadet

explanation.surface: A cadet role-played something, so it seemed.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the answer as wordplay (five letters 'out', jumbled) produces 'cadet'; 'apparently' flags the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: To act something out is to perform or represent it in mime or drama.

clue.text: Creature finding soldiers a source of food?

parts.words: finding soldiers a source of food
parts.note: soldiers are a caste of ants, and this creature lives by feeding on ants

explanation.surface: An animal that finds soldiers a good meal, sounding like a war monster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soldiers' sounds military, but soldier ants are the meal.
explanation.definitionFit: The anteater is a long-snouted mammal of the Americas, a creature that feeds on ants.

clue.text: Accept consequences and weep about a Republican prison

indicators.note: the weeping word is put round the next pieces, so about signals going around

parts.note: to weep is to cry
the can is slang for prison

explanation.surface: Someone has to take the blame and weeps over a Republican being jailed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the can' is American slang for prison.
explanation.definitionFit: To carry the can is a British idiom for taking the blame or responsibility for something.

clue.text: Adopt a son, setting up fast birds from down under

indicators.note: in a down clue, setting up means raising, so the birds' letters read upwards

parts.note: emus are swift flightless birds from Australia

explanation.surface: Adopting a son while setting up a fast-bird farm in Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: To assume a role or a name is to take it on, as to adopt it.

clue.text: Announce a line that must be crossed by crowd

indicators.note: the crowd crosses over the other pieces, so they end up inside it

parts.note: a herd is a crowd, often a disparaging one

explanation.surface: Announcing a boundary line that the crowd must cross.
explanation.definitionFit: To herald something is to proclaim or announce its coming.

clue.text: Lustre surrounding vacant blonde boozer

indicators.note: the lustre word goes round the next piece, so surrounding puts one inside the other

parts.note: lustre is a gleam or sheen

indicators.note: vacant means emptied, so only the outer letters of the word blonde remain

explanation.surface: A glamorous but empty-headed blonde in a pub, all shine and no substance.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'boozer' is British slang for a pub; 'vacant blonde' leaves B and E.
explanation.definitionFit: A shebeen is an unlicensed drinking den, especially in Ireland or South Africa, so a pub.

clue.text: Defiant words may see some miss other exit

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A defiant exit, storming out while the others watch.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition ran on to 'may see'; those words only link the definition to the hidden letters, and a defiant retort cannot mean 'may see'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a childish retort of defiance, said after having the last word.

clue.text: European energy needed to support southern ally

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece goes underneath, so the energy letter comes last

parts.note: to ally is to join or unite, to wed
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A European country's energy needed to back up a southern ally.
explanation.definitionFit: A Swede is a native of Sweden, and so a European.

clue.text: Heat and cut in pieces on your own

indicators.note: something in pieces is broken up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cooking instruction: heat something and cut it up, all by yourself.
explanation.definitionFit: Unattached means single or not linked to anyone, so alone or on your own.

clue.text: Pull back, adopting new custom

indicators.note: adopting means taking in, so one piece takes the other inside it
back is taken as backwards, so the pulling word is reversed

parts.note: to tow is to pull

explanation.surface: Someone pulls back from taking up a new habit.
explanation.definitionFit: Wont is an old noun for habit, so it means a usual practice or custom.

clue.text: Finished full of rage and put at risk

indicators.note: the finishing word is filled with another, so full of puts one inside the other

parts.note: finished means ended
rage is anger

explanation.surface: Someone was done in, full of fury and left in danger.
explanation.definitionFit: To endanger something is to expose it to harm, so endangered means at risk.

clue.text: Newspaper's start of sales pitch

definitions.note: read as 'Newspaper is', the 's joining definition to wordplay

indicators.note: start of takes only the opening letter of the word sales

parts.note: pitch is the black tar used on roads and ships

explanation.surface: A newspaper begins its sales pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Star is a British tabloid.
explanation.definitionFit: The Star is the name of several newspapers, including the British Daily Star.
